claim: Olfactory stimuli are first detected by a large family of olfactory receptors residing in the nasal epithelium.
source: Olfactory stimuli are first detected by a large family of olfactory receptors residing in the nasal epithelium (Buck and Axel, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buck and Axel, 1991

claim: Each odour molecule may activate a number of olfactory receptor types due to broad ligand-receptor binding.
source: Due to a broad ligand-receptor binding (Araneda et al., 2000; Del Mármol et al., 2021; Malnic et al., 1999), each odour molecule may activate a number of olfactory receptor types, leading to a combinatorial representation (Malnic et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Araneda et al., 2000; Del Mármol et al., 2021; Malnic et al., 1999

claim: Molecules may bind a common receptor, which can lead to antagonism depending on the efficacy.
source: For example, molecules may bind a common receptor, which, depending on the efficacy, can lead to antagonism (Cruz and Lowe, 2013; Kurahashi et al., 1994; Oka et al., 2004; Reddy et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2019) or enhancement (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cruz and Lowe, 2013; Kurahashi et al., 1994; Oka et al., 2004; Reddy et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2019

claim: Molecules binding a common receptor can lead to enhancement.
source: For example, molecules may bind a common receptor, which, depending on the efficacy, can lead to antagonism (Cruz and Lowe, 2013; Kurahashi et al., 1994; Oka et al., 2004; Reddy et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2019) or enhancement (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu et al., 2020

claim: Complex pharmacological interactions at olfactory receptors are a widespread phenomenon.
source: Recent large-scale studies demonstrate that this is a widespread phenomenon (Inagaki et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2020; Zak et al., 2020), which means that neural responses to mixtures often do not equal the sums of responses to the individual odours.
evidence: Supported by citations to Inagaki et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2020; Zak et al., 2020

claim: Neural responses to mixtures often do not equal the sums of responses to the individual odours.
source: Recent large-scale studies demonstrate that this is a widespread phenomenon (Inagaki et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2020; Zak et al., 2020), which means that neural responses to mixtures often do not equal the sums of responses to the individual odours.
evidence: Supported by citations to Inagaki et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2020; Zak et al., 2020, and logical inference from the widespread phenomenon

claim: There are many forms of nonlinear summation at multiple stages of olfactory processing, including the saturation of neural responses.
source: In addition to the interactions at the periphery, there are many forms of nonlinear summation at multiple stages of olfactory processing, including the saturation of neural responses (Firestein et al., 1993; Wachowiak and Cohen, 2001) and inhibitory interactions within the olfactory bulb (OB) (Economo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Firestein et al., 1993; Wachowiak and Cohen, 2001

claim: Inhibitory interactions within the olfactory bulb contribute to nonlinear summation.
source: In addition to the interactions at the periphery, there are many forms of nonlinear summation at multiple stages of olfactory processing, including the saturation of neural responses (Firestein et al., 1993; Wachowiak and Cohen, 2001) and inhibitory interactions within the olfactory bulb (OB) (Economo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Economo et al., 2016

claim: Widespread suppressive interactions are observed in the piriform cortex.
source: Widespread suppressive interactions are also observed in downstream areas, including the piriform cortex (Penker et al., 2020; Stettler and Axel, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Penker et al., 2020; Stettler and Axel, 2009

claim: Nonlinear summation of signals in primary sensory areas is sometimes considered information limiting.
source: However, in primary sensory areas, it is sometimes considered information limiting (Laughlin, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to Laughlin, 1989

claim: Nonlinear summations do not occur for all odour mixtures.
source: Nonlinear summations, or 'interactions', do not occur for all odour mixtures (Fletcher, 2011; Gupta et al., 2015; Tabor et al., 2004), but occur prevalently when the background and target activation patterns overlap.
evidence: Supported by citations to Fletcher, 2011; Gupta et al., 2015; Tabor et al., 2004

claim: Nonlinear summations occur prevalently when the background and target activation patterns overlap.
source: Nonlinear summations, or 'interactions', do not occur for all odour mixtures (Fletcher, 2011; Gupta et al., 2015; Tabor et al., 2004), but occur prevalently when the background and target activation patterns overlap.
evidence: Supported by citations to Fletcher, 2011; Gupta et al., 2015; Tabor et al., 2004

claim: Nonlinear summation happens when a mixture contains many components.
source: This happens when a mixture contains many components (Mathis et al., 2016), as well as when the background odours are structurally related to the target odour (Cruz and Lowe, 2013; Fletcher, 2011; Jinks and Laing, 1999; Kay et al., 2003; Mathis et al., 2016; Tabor et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mathis et al., 2016

claim: Nonlinear summation happens when the background odours are structurally related to the target odour.
source: This happens when a mixture contains many components (Mathis et al., 2016), as well as when the background odours are structurally related to the target odour (Cruz and Lowe, 2013; Fletcher, 2011; Jinks and Laing, 1999; Kay et al., 2003; Mathis et al., 2016; Tabor et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cruz and Lowe, 2013; Fletcher, 2011; Jinks and Laing, 1999; Kay et al., 2003; Mathis et al., 2016; Tabor et al., 2004

claim: Antagonism can reduce saturation-related loss of information.
source: Nonlinear summation poses a difficulty because it may distort a pattern of interest brought by non-uniform addition of unpredictable background patterns, although more recent studies suggest beneficial effects of antagonism, for example, by reducing saturation-related loss of information (Reddy et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reddy et al., 2018

claim: The olfactory system may not decompose mixture representations into component parts, but may solve the task by learning task-specific boundaries instead.
source: Due to this difficulty, some studies have suggested that the olfactory system may not decompose mixture representations into component parts, but may solve the task by learning task-specific boundaries instead (Mathis et al., 2016; Wilson and Stevenson, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mathis et al., 2016; Wilson and Stevenson, 2003

claim: Methyl butyrate (MB) responses overlap the most with the ethyl butyrate (EB) response patterns.
source: An analysis of glomerular activity patterns revealed that methyl butyrate (MB) responses overlap the most with the EB response patterns, followed by closely related esters (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by data from glomerular activity pattern analysis shown in Figure 1C-E

claim: The olfactometer is capable of presenting stable concentrations of odours for mixtures, with ionisation levels summing linearly when two odours are mixed.
source: We used a photoionisation detector to ensure that, when two odours are mixed, ionisation levels sum linearly (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by photoionisation detector measurements shown in Figure 2A-C

claim: A large proportion of M/T cells exhibited nonlinear summation (39.0% of M/T cells showed a deviation from linearity greater than 2).
source: As reported before, a large proportion of M/T cells exhibited nonlinear summation (39.0% of M/T cells showed a deviation from linearity greater than 2; 71/182 regions of interest [ROIs], seven fields of view, four mice; see Materials and methods) with a large fraction showing sublinear summation (35.7%, 65/182 ROIs).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from imaging experiments: 71/182 ROIs, seven fields of view, four mice

claim: A large fraction of M/T cells showed sublinear summation (35.7%, 65/182 ROIs).
source: As reported before, a large proportion of M/T cells exhibited nonlinear summation (39.0% of M/T cells showed a deviation from linearity greater than 2; 71/182 regions of interest [ROIs], seven fields of view, four mice; see Materials and methods) with a large fraction showing sublinear summation (35.7%, 65/182 ROIs).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from imaging experiments: 65/182 ROIs

claim: Mice learned to discriminate EB against other single odours, reaching an accuracy of 80% within 200 trials on average.
source: The mice learned to perform this task well, reaching an accuracy of 80% within 200 trials on average (Figure 3B and C; number of trials to reach 80% accuracy = 194.3 ± 21.9; n = 7 mice).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from 7 mice shown in Figure 3B and C

claim: Mice performed the mixture task at a high accuracy from the beginning (90.2% ± 1.3% of trials with correct responses in the first session).
source: The mice performed the mixture task at a high accuracy from the beginning (90.2% ± 1.3% of trials with correct responses in the first session; n = 7 mice).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from 7 mice in the first session

claim: Mice tended to lick more indiscriminately on MB-containing trials regardless of the presence of EB.
source: However, the mistakes they made were odour-specific, in that they tended to lick more indiscriminately on MB-containing trials regardless of the presence of EB (Figure 3D and E; mean lick preference index for MB trials = 0.74 ± 0.04 vs. 0.93 for five other background odours, p = 0.0035, one-way ANOVA; n = 7 mice).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing mean lick preference index for MB trials = 0.74 ± 0.04 vs. 0.93 for five other background odours, p = 0.0035, one-way ANOVA; n = 7 mice

claim: With training, the performance on MB trials became accurate, demonstrating that mice can learn to accurately detect the target odour in binary mixtures even when the background odour is similar.
source: However, with training, the performance on MB trials, too, became accurate, demonstrating that mice can learn to accurately detect the target odour in binary mixtures even when the background odour is similar.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing improvement in performance on MB trials with training

claim: M/T cells in behaving mice tended to sum mixture responses more linearly than when the mice were anaesthetised.
source: This revealed that the M/T cells in behaving mice tended to sum mixture responses more linearly than when the mice were anaesthetised (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data comparing behaving and anaesthetised conditions shown in Figure 4D

claim: In the anaesthetised case, the majority of the OB output neurons exhibit sublinear summation (median fractional deviation = –0.39).
source: In the anaesthetised case, a steep slope in the cumulative histogram occurs at a negative value (median fractional deviation = –0.39), indicating that the majority of the OB output neurons exhibit sublinear summation.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of fractional deviation data from anaesthetised mice

claim: M/T cells from behaving mice showed a broader distribution of fractional deviation centred around 0 (median fractional deviation = –0.12).
source: On the other hand, M/T cells from behaving mice showed a broader distribution centred around 0 (median fractional deviation = –0.12; P = 3.83 × 10–10, two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test comparing the behaving vs. anaesthetised data; n = 202 ROIs and 103 ROIs, respectively).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of fractional deviation data from behaving mice, with statistical comparison to anaesthetised data (P = 3.83 × 10–10, two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test; n = 202 ROIs and 103 ROIs)

claim: The difference in linearity of summation between behaving and anaesthetised mice was most striking in the first second after the odour onset ('early phase').
source: Using this index to compare the two conditions, we found that the difference was most striking in the first second after the odour onset ('early phase'; Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by time course analysis shown in Figure 4G

claim: Responses in the somata are more linear in the early phase compared to the apical dendrites.
source: Further, we observed that the responses in the somata are more linear in the early phase compared to the apical dendrites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by imaging data comparing somata and apical dendrites shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Dampened responses in the early phase of somatic responses may underlie the reduced mixture suppression.
source: These observations together may indicate that dampened responses in the early phase of somatic responses may underlie the reduced mixture suppression, although some contribution may come from more decorrelated responses at the somata (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from observations of dampened responses and reduced suppression, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The property of mixture summation is more linear in the awake, behaving mice.
source: Overall, the results indicate that the property of mixture summation is more linear in the awake, behaving mice, and that linearisation is not imprinted permanently as a result of learning.
evidence: Supported by comparison of imaging data from awake, behaving mice and anaesthetised mice

claim: Linearisation is not imprinted permanently as a result of learning.
source: Overall, the results indicate that the property of mixture summation is more linear in the awake, behaving mice, and that linearisation is not imprinted permanently as a result of learning.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of trained and anaesthetised conditions showing that linearity changes with state

claim: M/T cell responses are significantly smaller and more variable in awake, behaving mice compared to anaesthetised mice.
source: While the above result demonstrates that mixtures sum more linearly in awake, behaving mice, M/T cell responses are also significantly smaller and more variable in this condition.
evidence: Supported by analysis of trial-by-trial response similarity showing lower within-class correlation in behaving mice

claim: In the anaesthetised mice, the M/T cell response patterns are highly correlated, both within class and across classes.
source: This showed that, in the anaesthetised mice, the M/T cell response patterns are highly correlated, both within class (comparison between trials with EB) and across classes (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: In the awake, behaving mice, responses were less consistent, indicated by the lower within-class correlation.
source: In the awake, behaving mice, as expected, responses were less consistent, indicated by the lower within-class correlation (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: Across-class patterns were substantially less correlated in behaving mice, suggesting S+ responses may be more discriminable.
source: However, because across-class patterns were substantially less correlated (Figure 5A and B), S+ responses may be more discriminable in the behaving mice.
evidence: Inferred from correlation analysis showing lower across-class correlation in behaving mice, shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: M/T cells from anaesthetised mice showed better discriminability initially, but later, M/T cells in the behaving mice performed as well as the anaesthetised mice.
source: This indicated that M/T cells from anaesthetised mice showed better discriminability initially, but later, M/T cells in the behaving mice performed as well as the anaesthetised mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by discriminability index analysis over time shown in Figure 5C

claim: M/T cells from the two conditions (behaving and anaesthetised) performed similarly for the first 1 s when using SVMs to discriminate S+ vs S- responses.
source: This time, M/T cells from the two conditions performed similarly for the first 1 s, performing above chance soon after the odour onset (earliest time where accuracy is significantly above 0.5 = 0.67 s for the behaving case, and 1.12 s for anaesthetised data; t-test at a significance level of 0.05; n = 13 fields of view, six mice for behaving case; 8 fields of view, four mice for the anaesthetised case; Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by SVM decoding analysis shown in Figure 5D, with statistical testing (t-test at significance level of 0.05; n = 13 fields of view, six mice for behaving case; 8 fields of view, four mice for anaesthetised case)

claim: The data from behaving mice outperformed the anaesthetised case in the later phase (median accuracy for 2–3 s after odour onset = 0.58 vs. 0.70 for anaesthetised vs. behaving mice, respectively; p = 0.027).
source: Further, the data from behaving mice outperformed the anaesthetised case in the later phase (median accuracy for 2–3 s after odour onset = 0.58 vs. 0.70 for anaesthetised vs. behaving mice, respectively; p = 0.027, Mann–Whitney U test for equal medians).
evidence: Supported by SVM decoding analysis with statistical testing (p = 0.027, Mann–Whitney U test for equal medians)

claim: Over time, mixture responses come to resemble the target component odour pattern more in the awake, behaving mice than in the anaesthetised mice.
source: This may suggest that, over time, mixture responses come to resemble the target component odour pattern more in the awake, behaving mice than in the anaesthetised mice.
evidence: Inferred from SVM analysis where training on single odours and testing on mixtures showed better performance in behaving mice in the late phase

claim: The time course of decoder accuracy did not strictly depend on the linearity of mixture summation.
source: Curiously, the time course of decoder accuracy did not strictly depend on the linearity of mixture summation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by comparison of decoder accuracy and linearity shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: Despite the substantial differences in the amplitudes and variability of responses, M/T cells in behaving mice are able to encode the presence of the target odour well.
source: Overall, the result suggests that, despite the substantial differences in the amplitudes and variability of responses, M/T cells in behaving mice are able to encode the presence of the target odour well.
evidence: Inferred from SVM decoding results showing good discriminability in behaving mice despite smaller and more variable responses

claim: EB and MB mixtures are represented equally linearly in naïve but awake, head-fixed mice regardless of engagement level.
source: In all awake conditions, we found the EB and MB responses to sum equally linearly (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that the linearity of summation does not depend on the behavioural states or learning.
evidence: Supported by imaging data from naïve engaged and disengaged mice shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The linearity of summation does not depend on the behavioural states or learning.
source: In all awake conditions, we found the EB and MB responses to sum equally linearly (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that the linearity of summation does not depend on the behavioural states or learning.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of linearity across trained, naïve engaged, and naïve disengaged conditions shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The ability to analyse mixtures in terms of the constituents was particularly poor for the disengaged mice.
source: However, the performance of SVMs on these datasets showed a state-dependence. While the general ability to discriminate S+ vs. S- odours was comparable across the states, the ability to analyse mixtures in terms of the constituents – SVMs trained on single odours and tested on mixture patterns – was particularly poor for the disengaged mice (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: Supported by SVM decoding analysis comparing trained, naïve engaged, and naïve disengaged mice shown in Figure 6C-F

claim: The ability to correctly decode the presence of an odour does not strictly correlate with the linearity of mixture summation.
source: Since the linearity of summation was comparable across the three groups (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), this, again, suggests that the ability to correctly decode the presence of an odour does not strictly correlate with the linearity of mixture summation.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of linearity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and decoder performance (Figure 6C-F) across behavioral states

claim: In all cases, the decoder performed most accurately in the late phase.
source: In all cases, the decoder performed most accurately in the late phase.
evidence: Supported by SVM decoding analysis showing peak accuracy in late phase across all conditions

claim: When the data from the anaesthetised mice was used, normalising sublinearity was particularly detrimental around 2 s after the odour onset.
source: When the data from the anaesthetised mice was used, normalising sublinearity was particularly detrimental around 2 s after the odour onset (Figure 7C), qualitatively reproducing the transient decrease in the accuracy seen with the observed mixture responses (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7C

claim: With the data from the behaving mice, normalising sublinearity did not have as significant an effect on the mixture discriminability, even in the late stage when sublinear summation becomes more widespread.
source: In contrast, with the data from the behaving mice, normalising sublinearity did not have as significant an effect on the mixture discriminability, even in the late stage when sublinear summation becomes more widespread (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7D and E

claim: The functional consequence of nonlinear summation may depend on specific circumstances, for example, on how separable, or decorrelated, the activity patterns are.
source: Thus, the functional consequence of nonlinear summation may depend on specific circumstances, for example, on how separable, or decorrelated, the activity patterns are.
evidence: Inferred from simulation results showing different effects of sublinearity on anaesthetised vs. behaving data

claim: Mixture responses in the OB are highly state-dependent and evolve over time.
source: Overall, our result indicates that mixture responses in the OB are highly state-dependent and evolve over time (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by comparison of mixture responses across different behavioral states and time points shown in Figure 6F

claim: The signal summation in the primary olfactory area of the mouse is significantly more linear in awake mice.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the signal summation in the primary olfactory area of the mouse is significantly more linear in awake mice.
evidence: Supported by imaging data comparing awake and anaesthetised mice

claim: Many previous studies reported that suppressive mixture interactions are widespread in the central nervous system, based on anaesthetised preparations.
source: This is notable because many previous studies reported that suppressive mixture interactions are widespread in the central nervous system, based on anaesthetised preparations (Bell et al., 1987; Cruz and Lowe, 2013; Penker et al., 2020; Stettler and Axel, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bell et al., 1987; Cruz and Lowe, 2013; Penker et al., 2020; Stettler and Axel, 2009

claim: The ability to discriminate binary mixture responses does not correlate strictly with linearity in summation.
source: However, our analysis also indicates that the ability to discriminate binary mixture responses does not correlate strictly with linearity in summation.
evidence: Supported by analysis showing decoder performance peaks when mixture responses were most sublinear in behaving mice

claim: The behavioural improvement was not accompanied by more linear summation.
source: First, the behavioural improvement was not accompanied by more linear summation.
evidence: Supported by comparison of linearity across trained and naïve conditions showing no difference

claim: The time course of decoder accuracy does not follow the linearity of summation.
source: Second, the time course of decoder accuracy does not follow the linearity of summation.
evidence: Supported by comparison of decoder accuracy time course and linearity time course

claim: In the data from behaving mice, the decoder performance peaked when mixture responses were most sublinear.
source: Indeed, in the data from behaving mice, the decoder performance peaked when mixture responses were most sublinear.
evidence: Supported by analysis of decoder performance and linearity over time in behaving mice

claim: A sublinear mixture summation due to saturating influences limits the discriminability of mixture responses.
source: Our simple simulation indicates that, generally, a sublinear mixture summation due to saturating influences limits the discriminability of mixture responses.
evidence: Supported by simulation results showing reduced discriminability with normalising sublinearity

claim: Dampened responses in awake animals bring some advantage by maintaining the mixture responses in the linear range.
source: Thus, dampened responses in awake animals bring some advantage by maintaining the mixture responses in the linear range.
evidence: Inferred from observation of more linear summation in awake mice and simulation showing benefits of linearity

claim: In the behaving mice, even when the responses became larger at a later phase, the saturating influence was less detrimental to discrimination.
source: However, in the behaving mice, even when the responses became larger at a later phase, the saturating influence was less detrimental to discrimination.
evidence: Supported by simulation results showing less impact of sublinearity on behaving mice data

claim: Decorrelated response patterns may play a crucial role in enhancing classifier or behavioural performances.
source: Here, decorrelated response patterns may play a more crucial role as this is known to enhance classifier or behavioural performances (Bhattacharjee et al., 2019; Friedrich and Wiechert, 2014; Gschwend et al., 2015; Padmanabhan and Urban, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bhattacharjee et al., 2019; Friedrich and Wiechert, 2014; Gschwend et al., 2015; Padmanabhan and Urban, 2010

claim: Animals make accurate decisions within 1 s (771 ± 97 ms) of stimulus onset in the behavioral task described in this study.
source: While the behavioural task described in this study is simple and animals make accurate decisions within 1 s (771 ± 97 ms) of stimulus onset, the slower mechanisms described here may be important when larger and more reliable responses are required for accurate decisions.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing decision times of 771 ± 97 ms

claim: The ability to accurately analyse mixtures based on the knowledge of component is hypothesised to involve the piriform cortex, through learned representations.
source: Mechanistically, the ability to accurately analyse, or discriminate between, mixtures based on the knowledge of component is hypothesised to involve the piriform cortex, through learned representations (Chapuis and Wilson, 2011; Grabska-Barwińska et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chapuis and Wilson, 2011; Grabska-Barwińska et al., 2017

claim: For tufted cells, the relevant sources of feedback could be other brain regions, such as the anterior olfactory nucleus.
source: For tufted cells, however, the relevant sources of feedback could be other brain regions, such as the anterior olfactory nucleus (Chae et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chae et al., 2020

claim: Mixtures of odours often have qualities that are different from those of the individual components.
source: Mixtures of odours often have qualities that are different from those of the individual components.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about olfactory mixture perception

claim: For untrained subjects, olfactory mixtures that contain about 30 components tend to smell alike.
source: For untrained subjects, olfactory mixtures that contain about 30 components tend to smell alike (Weiss et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weiss et al., 2012

claim: Highly trained people like perfumers can only accurately identify individual components if unfamiliar mixtures contained no more than five components.
source: Even highly trained people like perfumers can only accurately identify individual components if unfamiliar mixtures contained no more than five components (Poupon et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Poupon et al., 2018

claim: In non-expert humans and rodents, when the task is to look for a particular aroma in the mixture, the tendency is to falsely report the presence of the target odour in target-odour detection tasks.
source: In addition, in non-expert humans and rodents alike, when the task is to look for a particular aroma in the mixture, the tendency is to falsely report the presence of the target odour in target-odour detection tasks (Laing and Glemarec, 1992; Rokni et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Laing and Glemarec, 1992; Rokni et al., 2014

claim: Extensive training for specific odours can improve the ability to detect the target odour.
source: In all cases, an extensive training for specific odours can improve the ability to detect the target odour, as seen in the case for sommeliers who routinely analyse key components in wines, which can contain several hundred component mixtures (Ilc et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ilc et al., 2016

claim: Training in specific odours seems to be key to improving on mixture analysis.
source: Thus, while mixture perception is highly context specific (Rokni and Murthy, 2014), training in specific odours seems to be key to improving on mixture analysis.
evidence: Inferred from examples of trained individuals (perfumers, sommeliers) performing better, with citation to Rokni and Murthy, 2014

claim: With more complex mixtures, mechanisms within the OB may reach a limit, and also is unlikely to be the only mechanism that is used to solve the task.
source: With more complex mixtures, mechanisms within the OB may reach a limit, and also is unlikely to be the only mechanism that is used to solve the task.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the complexity of mixture processing

claim: Mixture summation is more linear in the early phase of evoked responses in awake, head-fixed mice performing an odour detection task, due to dampened responses.
source: Here, we investigate how the olfactory system deals with binary mixtures of odours under different brain states by two-photon imaging of olfactory bulb (OB) output neurons. Unlike previous studies using anaesthetised animals, we found that mixture summation is more linear in the early phase of evoked responses in awake, head-fixed mice performing an odour detection task, due to dampened responses.
evidence: Supported by imaging data comparing awake and anaesthetised mice

claim: Despite smaller and more variable responses, decoding analyses indicated that the data from behaving mice was well discriminable.
source: Despite smaller and more variable responses, decoding analyses indicated that the data from behaving mice was well discriminable.
evidence: Supported by SVM decoding analysis on data from behaving mice

claim: Learning to accurately perform the mixture detection task is not accompanied by more linear mixture summation.
source: Further, a comparison with naïve mice indicated that learning to accurately perform the mixture detection task is not accompanied by more linear mixture summation.
evidence: Supported by comparison of linearity between trained and naïve mice

claim: Saturating sublinearity tends to degrade the discriminability, but the extent of the impairment may depend on other factors, including pattern decorrelation.
source: Finally, using a simulation, we demonstrate that, while saturating sublinearity tends to degrade the discriminability, the extent of the impairment may depend on other factors, including pattern decorrelation.
evidence: Supported by simulation results showing different effects of sublinearity depending on conditions

claim: The mixture representation in the primary olfactory area is state-dependent.
source: Altogether, our results demonstrate that the mixture representation in the primary olfactory area is state-dependent, but the analytical perception may not strictly correlate with linearity in summation.
evidence: Supported by comparison of mixture representations across different behavioral states

claim: The analytical perception may not strictly correlate with linearity in summation.
source: Altogether, our results demonstrate that the mixture representation in the primary olfactory area is state-dependent, but the analytical perception may not strictly correlate with linearity in summation.
evidence: Supported by analysis showing decoder performance does not follow linearity of summation

claim: Tbx21Cre::Ai95D mice express the calcium indicator GCaMP6f in M/T cells.
source: Using a two-photon microscope, we imaged from the glomerular layer of the OB in Tbx21Cre::Ai95D mice, which express the calcium indicator GCaMP6f (Dana et al., 2019) in M/T cells (Haddad et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dana et al., 2019 and Haddad et al., 2013

claim: The masking index measures the amount of overlap in response patterns between the target odour and background odours and correlates well with behavioural performances.
source: According to Rokni et al., the masking index, which measures the amount of overlap in response patterns between the target odour and background odours, correlates well with behavioural performances (Rokni et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rokni et al., 2014

claim: Olfactory figure-ground segregation is most difficult when the target and background odours evoke overlapping activity patterns.
source: Olfactory figure-ground segregation is most difficult when the target and background odours evoke overlapping activity patterns (Rokni et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rokni et al., 2014
